options.metric: Mean reported casualties per crash, calculated as number_of_persons_injured + number_of_persons_killed
options.denominator: Crashes with both person outcome counts present in the same time group
options.reason: A casualty-per-crash mean directly describes how severe police-reported crashes were, conditional on a crash occurring.
options.answer: NYC police-reported crashes averaged 0.409 injured or killed people at night versus 0.315 by day in 2013-2025, about 30% more per crash, but without traffic or travel exposure the data cannot establish whether NYC streets are more dangerous at night overall.
options.interpretation: This framing addresses whether nighttime crashes were more severe by comparing injured plus killed people per crash, with Night defined as 21:00-05:59 and Day as 06:00-20:59 across 2013-2025; the denominator is crashes with both outcome counts present. Night averaged 0.409 reported casualties per crash versus 0.315 by day, so the chart indicates greater casualty burden conditional on a police-reported crash, a defensible measure of crash severity. It does not establish whether a person, trip, or mile of travel is riskier at night because traffic and travel exposure are not in the data. The check found partial coverage for 2012 (July-December) and 2026 (January-June; 8,877/36,424 or 24.37% missing death counts), so those years were excluded; 42/2,132,218 (0.001970%) 2013-2025 rows missing an outcome count were excluded, and 23,786 (1.115574%) selected records at valid 00:00 times were retained as night despite possible default coding (no selected crash times were missing).

options.metric: Percentage of crashes with at least one person injured or killed, using number_of_persons_injured + number_of_persons_killed > 0
options.denominator: All crashes with both person outcome counts present in the same time group
options.reason: The share of crashes involving any casualty focuses on how frequently a reported crash caused harm, rather than the number of casualties in a crash.
options.answer: A higher share of NYC police-reported crashes involved injury or death at night than by day in 2013-2025 (28.3% versus 23.7%), but without traffic or travel exposure the data cannot establish whether NYC streets are more dangerous at night overall.
options.interpretation: This framing addresses how often a police-reported crash involved harm by comparing the percentage with at least one injured or killed person, where Night is 21:00-05:59 and Day is 06:00-20:59 over 2013-2025; the denominator is all crashes with both person outcome counts present. The chart shows a casualty in 28.3% of nighttime crashes and 23.7% of daytime crashes, a 4.6 percentage-point difference; this is defensible as a measure of the frequency of harmful crashes conditional on a crash. It does not show whether a person, trip, or mile of travel faces more danger at night because the data have no traffic or travel-exposure denominator. The check found partial coverage for 2012 (July-December) and 2026 (January-June; 8,877/36,424 or 24.37% missing death counts), so those years were excluded; 42/2,132,218 (0.001970%) 2013-2025 rows missing an outcome count were excluded, and 23,786 (1.115574%) selected records at valid 00:00 times were retained as night despite possible default coding (no selected crash times were missing).
